q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE reason why the United States intervened in Vietnam after 1954.
parts.b: Explain ONE reason why the United States failed to defeat North Vietnam despite its military superiority, using the historian's interpretation in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way in which the Vietnam War affected the United States domestically.

sample_answers.a: American leaders believed in the 'domino theory' — that if Vietnam fell to communism, the rest of Southeast Asia would follow — so they committed advisers, then troops, to prevent a communist victory.
sample_answers.b: According to the passage, the war was a political struggle for Vietnamese nationalism that American firepower could not resolve; the Viet Cong and North Vietnamese endured enormous losses because they were fighting for national unification, while the South Vietnamese government never won its people's loyalty.
sample_answers.c: The war divided American society, sparking mass protests, undermining trust in government (especially after the Tet Offensive contradicted official claims of progress), and creating a lasting reluctance to commit ground troops abroad — the 'Vietnam syndrome.'

q1.stimulus:
Historians explain America's defeat in Vietnam as a failure to understand the nature of the war. The United States fought it as a Cold War battle against communist aggression, pouring in over half a million troops and unmatched firepower. But for the Vietnamese communists, it was a war of national liberation — the latest phase of a decades-long struggle against foreign domination, first French and then American. The South Vietnamese government, meanwhile, was corrupt and lacked popular support, so American power was propping up a regime that could not stand on its own. Superior technology, including helicopters and massive bombing, could destroy villages and kill soldiers, but it could not create a legitimate government in Saigon or break the determination of an enemy fighting for national unification.
—Historian's account of the Vietnam War in the period c. 1900–present

q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE power the resolution grants to the President.
parts.b: Describe ONE way in which the resolution changed the constitutional balance of war powers.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why Congress passed the resolution with almost no opposition in 1964.

sample_answers.a: The resolution authorizes the President to 'take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack' and 'to prevent further aggression' — effectively a blank check for military escalation in Vietnam.
sample_answers.b: It transferred the decision for war from Congress (which the Constitution gives the power to declare war) to the President, allowing massive escalation without a formal declaration of war.
sample_answers.c: In the charged atmosphere after the reported Tonkin attacks, with an election approaching, few politicians wanted to appear soft on communism; the administration presented the resolution as a routine show of resolve, and most members did not foresee it enabling a full-scale war.

q2.stimulus:
Resolved by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That the Congress approves and supports the determination of the President, as Commander in Chief, to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression. ... The United States is, therefore, prepared, as the President determines, to take all necessary steps, including the use of armed force, to assist any member or protocol state of the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty requesting assistance in defense of its freedom.
—Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, U.S. Congress, 7 August 1964

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the helicopter that made it important in the Vietnam War.
parts.b: Explain ONE way in which helicopter warfare reflected the American strategy in Vietnam.
parts.c: Explain ONE reason why technological advantages such as helicopters did not produce an American victory.

sample_answers.a: The UH-1 'Huey' could transport troops rapidly across Vietnam's roadless terrain, evacuate wounded, and provide air support — giving American forces unprecedented mobility in a country with few usable roads.
sample_answers.b: Helicopters embodied the American strategy of attrition and mobility: using technology to find and destroy enemy forces quickly, minimizing American casualties while maximizing firepower — a strategy suited to conventional battle but not to political warfare.
sample_answers.c: Helicopters could win battles but not the political struggle; they could not make the South Vietnamese government legitimate, stop North Vietnamese infiltration, or defeat an enemy willing to absorb enormous losses for national unification.

q3.stimulus: The photograph shows a U.S. Army UH-1B 'Huey' helicopter taking off after completing a mission during the Vietnam War. The Huey became the iconic aircraft of the war: the United States deployed thousands of helicopters for troop transport, medical evacuation, and air assault. The image, from U.S. Army sources via the National Archives, illustrates the American military's reliance on air mobility in a war fought across difficult terrain.
